entities.summary:
Count Alajos Károlyi de Nagykároly (1825–1889) was a pivotal Austro-Hungarian diplomat whose career spanned the tumultuous mid-19th century, witnessing the decline of Austrian influence in Germany and the consolidation of the Dual Monarchy. As Imperial Ambassador to Prussia during the critical years leading up to the Austro-Prussian War and later to the newly unified German Empire, he navigated the complex geopolitical shifts that redefined Central Europe. His subsequent seventeen-year tenure as Ambassador to the Court of St. James's in London established him as a key figure in Austro-British relations and a central observer of the Eastern Question. Károlyi's diplomatic efforts were instrumental in shaping the foreign policy of the Habsburg monarchy during a period of profound internal and external transformation.

Károlyi began his diplomatic career in the 1840s, serving in various minor posts before his crucial appointment as Ambassador to Prussia in 1866. Arriving just prior to the outbreak of the Austro-Prussian War, he was immediately thrust into negotiations that culminated in the Peace of Prague in August 1866, which formally excluded Austria from German affairs and paved the way for the North German Confederation. After the unification of Germany, he served as Ambassador to the German Empire from 1866 to 1871. In 1871, he was transferred to London, where he represented Austria-Hungary until 1888, becoming the longest-serving ambassador there. During his London posting, Károlyi played a significant role in the Congress of Berlin in 1878, where he helped solidify the Great Powers' arrangement for the Balkans following the Russo-Turkish War.
